The county museum opened its new wing on a grey morning in late autumn, and by noon the halls were full of school groups. The building itself is unremarkable: a long brick block with tall windows, a slate roof, and a portico added in the nineteen twenties. Inside, however, the collection is anything but ordinary. Row after row of wooden cases hold shells, minerals, pressed plants, and the mounted skins of birds collected by amateur naturalists over more than a century. Many of the labels are handwritten in faded ink, and some of the older specimens have lost their original tags altogether.

The director, a quiet woman who joined the museum after twenty years of fieldwork in the marshes, led the visitors through the first gallery herself. She explained that the museum began as a private cabinet in a merchant's house, grew through donations, and nearly closed twice during the last century when money ran short. The current renovation, she said, was paid for primarily by a single bequest, and the new wing was designed to let the collection breathe: better air, softer light, and cases that can be opened without moving an entire display.

In the second gallery the exhibits turn to the study of birds. Here the curators have arranged a long case of the small songbirds that pass through the region each spring. The plumage of the males varies from dull olive to a bright yellow, and the labels note the date and place of each capture. A separate case holds a single egg, pale and speckled, found in a hollow tree in the nineteen fifties. The shell has a small cavity near one end, which the label attributes to a predator, though no one now remembers which one.

The third gallery is the newest and, for most visitors, the strangest. It is devoted to the instruments that naturalists used in the field: brass microscopes, glass slides, spirit levels, and a heavy wooden box of the kind once used to carry a sample back from a distant valley. Beside the box sits a notebook with water stains on almost every page. The entries are mostly short, and many are hard to read, but a few pages record the weather, the hour, and the color of the soil, as though the writer were afraid of losing any detail at all.

Near the end of the hall, a case of polished stones explains how the region's geology was mapped. The rocks are not valuable, but they are old, and the labels describe how each layer formed under heat and pressure. One display shows a thin section of sandstone mounted on a glass slide; under the lens the grains look like a heap of broken glass. A second display explains that the whole valley rests on a deep substrate of limestone, laid down when the area was covered by a shallow sea.

The museum staff seem aware that most visitors come for the birds and leave before the geology. They have tried, with some success, to slow people down. Benches face the long cases, and the labels now ask questions as often as they give answers. Others, according to the director, prefer the quiet rooms at the back, where nothing is displayed at all and the drawers can be opened by appointment. Damage from damp has been a problem in those drawers, she admits, and the repair work is slow and expensive.

Below the main floor, in the basement, there is a small workshop where the worst of the damage is treated before an object goes back on display. The work is mostly done by volunteers, and the director says the museum could not manage without them.
